transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I went back and forth for weeks about whether I should even make this appointment. Because, you know, I’m a secondary school teacher—I teach sophomores mostly—and the workload is always incredibly overwhelming with the lesson planning and the grading and the parent emails that just never seem to stop. So for a while, I just told myself I was dealing with the usual stress of the school year. 

But... it’s not just that anymore. I’m here because I’ve started catching myself having these really unsettling thoughts. Like, I’ll get into bed at the end of the day, just completely drained, and I'll catch myself genuinely thinking that it would be so much easier if I just didn’t wake up the next morning. Just so I wouldn't have to face it all again. And then there’s my commute—I have this long drive home every afternoon, and I’ll just be sitting there behind the wheel, staring at the road, and I start wondering whether my family and my students would actually just be better off without me. Like I’m just this disappointment or a burden to everyone. And it really, really scares me that my brain is going there. I don’t want to act on it, I promise I don't, but the fact that these thoughts keep creeping in while I'm just driving down the highway... I just knew I needed to talk to someone because I don't trust why my mind is doing this.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things the way you used to, like activities you used to look forward to?

Yeah, actually... that’s exactly what’s happening, and it’s been really bothering me. I used to have all these things that kept me going, you know? Like, I play in this community softball league every Thursday evening. It used to be my favorite part of the week—just getting out there, laughing with the girls, burning off the stress from teaching. But lately, I’ve been canceling on them constantly. I’ll literally be sitting on my couch, fully dressed in my uniform, and I just... I can't make myself walk out the door because it just doesn't sound fun anymore. I just text them an excuse. 

And it’s not just softball. I’ve been in this book club for three years, and normally I'm the one leading the discussion, but the last few times I actually forced myself to go, I was just completely going through the motions. I just sat there staring at my glass of wine, not really listening or participating, because I just didn't care about the book or the conversation. I even stopped tending to my garden, which is usually my absolute sanctuary on Saturday mornings. I have these raised beds with tomatoes and zucchini and a whole herb section, and I used to love getting my hands in the dirt, but now the weeds are just taking over because the thought of going out there just feels like a massive chore. 

Even at school, it's bleeding into things there. I sponsor the robotics club, which I used to look forward to so much because the kids are so brilliant and funny, and seeing them figure out a problem used to be so rewarding. Now I just sit at my desk in the back of the room while they build things, just watching the clock, waiting for it to be over so I can go home. It’s like everything that used to give me a little spark or make me feel alive is just... flat. I either cancel my plans or I just fake my way through them, because none of it actually feels enjoyable anymore. And I don't understand why I can't just snap out of it and enjoy my life again, because I *want* to care about my tomatoes and my students' robots, I really do, but the feeling is just... gone.
Have you noticed that you're feeling more tired or lacking energy, even after a full night's sleep?

Oh, my gosh, yes. It doesn't even seem to matter how much I sleep anymore. I could be in bed for eight or nine hours—I'm actually getting into bed by like 9 PM most nights now just because I can't keep my eyes open—but then my alarm goes off at 6 AM and I feel like I haven't slept a wink. I wake up feeling like I ran a marathon in my sleep, just completely drained before my feet even hit the floor. 

And then I have to drag myself to school and put on that energetic teacher face for the sophomores, which takes everything out of me. By the time I actually get through a full day of teaching, and then if we have a department meeting after school—which we do every Tuesday and sometimes Thursdays, and they always run late because the head of the English department loves to hear himself talk—by the time I get through all of that, my body feels so incredibly heavy. Like my limbs are literally made of lead or wet sand or something. 

I'll finally get home and walk through the front door, and just the thought of doing normal, everyday tasks is completely overwhelming. Even just making dinner—and I'm talking about something so basic, like boiling water for pasta or throwing a frozen pizza in the oven—or sitting down to answer just a few parent emails... it honestly feels like climbing a massive hill. It feels physically impossible. And the emails are usually just simple things, you know, a parent asking about a missing assignment or a due date, things that used to take me two minutes to reply to. But I'll sit there staring at my laptop screen and I just do not have the physical energy to type the words. I just can't do it. I used to meal prep every Sunday, I'd have all these nice healthy lunches and dinners portioned out for the week in little glass containers, but now I'm just ordering takeout or eating cereal for dinner because standing at the stove requires energy I just don't have. It's this deep, deep exhaustion in my bones that just never goes away, no matter how much I rest.
Have you found yourself feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, rather than just occasionally feeling this way?

Well, honestly, I don't know if "depressed" or "down" is really the right word for it. I mean, when I hear the word depressed, I usually picture someone who is just crying all the time, you know? Like they're weeping into their pillow or they can't stop sobbing in their car. And I'm really not doing that at all. I don't actually feel sad, exactly. It’s not this heavy, sorrowful feeling where I want to cry about my life. 

It's honestly more like... I just feel completely blank. Just nothing. Like, for example, during my planning period—I have fourth period planning this semester, which is right before the lunch rush, so the halls are usually pretty quiet—I’ll just sit there at my desk with my red grading pen in my hand, staring at the whiteboard or looking out the window at the student parking lot, and I'm not feeling actively miserable or blue. I'm just... existing. It’s like the volume on all my emotions has just been turned all the way down to zero. 

I was actually trying to explain this to my mom on the phone last weekend, because she kept asking me, "Honey, why are you so sad lately? You sound so down," and I kept having to tell her, "Mom, I'm not sad!" I'm really not. I don't feel like I'm walking around with this dark raincloud of sadness over my head every day. It’s just that completely flat, empty feeling I was talking about before, where I'm just going through the motions of teaching and coming home and staring at the wall. So, no, I wouldn't really say I feel down or depressed most of the day... just hollow, I guess? If that makes any sense.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the lack of enjoyment in activities and the constant exhaustion?

Oh, wow, let me think... it's actually been quite a while now. If I look back at the calendar... yeah, it's been about a year and seven months. 

I know exactly when it started, too, because it was right when the district decided they needed to completely overhaul our testing standards. They asked me—well, "asked" is a strong word, it was more like they voluntold me—to take over the STEM assessment redesign. And at the time, I thought, okay, this is a great step for my career, maybe it'll lead to a department head position eventually, you know? But the thing is, they didn't give me any extra planning periods or a reduced course load to accommodate it. None of that. 

So I was doing this massive, district-wide redesign—creating all these new rubrics, aligning every single project with the new state mandates, sitting in endless Zoom meetings with the curriculum coordinators—all completely on top of my regular teaching load. I was still teaching five sections of sophomores, still grading all their labs, still trying to keep up with everything else... and it just broke me, I think. 

At first, I just thought I was burned out from the extra hours, you know, staying up until midnight working on spreadsheets and then waking up at 5 AM to lesson plan. But even after the heavy lifting for the redesign was finally over and that project wrapped up, the exhaustion just... it never went away. And that blank feeling I was telling you about just sort of settled in permanently. It’s just so frustrating because I used to pride myself on being the teacher who could juggle everything, the one the principal could always rely on to take on extra duties, and now here I am, a year and seven months later, and I'm still just... stuck like this. I keep wondering if I should have just said no to the committee, but you can't really say no in education without looking like you're not a team player, you know? So I just took it all on, and... yeah, that's exactly when all of this really started. About a year and seven months ago.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently, like losing or gaining a lot without trying?

Actually, yeah... I have. It's, um, it's been losing weight, mostly. And it's definitely not on purpose, I promise you that. I'm not doing one of those trendy diets or counting macros or anything like that. 

It's just... well, most school days, I completely forget to eat, or I just kind of avoid it altogether until late in the afternoon. Like, I was mentioning my fourth-period planning earlier, right? Well, fifth period is technically my designated lunch block, and normally I'd go down to the teacher's lounge, maybe heat up some leftovers, chat with the history teachers... but lately, the thought of eating just feels like another overwhelming chore. So I'll just stay in my classroom with the door closed and the lights off, just sitting there at my desk. I won't even realize I haven't had a single bite of food until maybe 4:00 or 4:30 when I'm finally driving home. Sometimes I don't even feel hungry then, I just suddenly realize, oh, I haven't actually chewed anything since yesterday. 

And because of that, over the past year or so, my clothes have gotten noticeably looser. It's really obvious, actually. I have these black trousers that I wear all the time for work—they used to fit perfectly, maybe even a little snug sometimes, you know? But now I have to wear a belt with them on the tightest notch, and they still kind of bunch up weirdly at the waist and hang off my legs. I was putting on a dress last week for our spring academic assembly, and it just hung off me like a sack. I had to go dig through the back of my closet to find a cardigan to wrap around it so I didn't look completely ridiculous in front of the students. It's just strange because, like I said, I haven't been trying to lose weight at all, not even a little bit. I just... I just don't have the drive to eat during the day anymore, and it's definitely showing on my body.
